name: THE FLEETWOOD JACK BURGER (comes with sweet little fries pies, jack cheese)

recipe.history:
Monterey Jack cheese is one of the few major cheeses with an origin story firmly rooted in American soil, specifically in the Monterey Bay area of California. Its history begins with the Spanish Franciscan and Dominican missionaries who arrived in California in the eighteenth century and established a tradition of mild, fresh-pressed cow's milk cheese in their missions — a style common to much of Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula. The commercial development of what we now recognize as Monterey Jack is attributed to a Scottish immigrant and businessman named David Jack, who in the 1880s began mass-producing and distributing a semi-firm, mild, high-moisture cheese from the Monterey region to markets throughout California. He stamped his name and shipping address on the rounds, and the cheese became known commercially as 'Jack's cheese from Monterey' — eventually shortened to 'Monterey Jack' or simply 'Jack cheese.' The cheese is characterized by its very mild, milky, slightly buttery flavor, its exceptionally high meltability, and its open, slightly springy texture. It melts faster and more smoothly than almost any other semi-firm cheese, making it a natural in quesadillas, enchiladas, and of course burgers. Pepper Jack, a variant spiced with jalapeños and other peppers, became enormously popular in the American Southwest and is now ubiquitous nationwide.

The idea of putting french fries on a burger is one of those inspired pieces of American ingenuity that sounds slightly absurd until you eat it, at which point it seems completely inevitable. The practice is most closely associated with Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where the Primanti Brothers sandwich — first served in the 1930s to truck drivers and market workers who needed a complete meal they could eat one-handed — featured french fries and coleslaw loaded directly into the sandwich. The concept spread through American regional food culture, and by the 2000s, fries-in-burger had become a celebrated variation at high-end and casual restaurants alike. Mini fries — bite-sized, crispy, sometimes formed into little 'pie' shapes using a mold — take this concept to its logical extreme: the crunch and salt and potato starch of a perfectly fried chip, compressed into the burger itself, providing textural contrast with every bite. The combination of Monterey Jack's mild creaminess, melted over a medium-rare patty, with the crunch of mini fry 'pies' on top is simultaneously playful and genuinely delicious.

The first time I put french fries inside a burger I was sixteen, at a diner in my hometown that had a self-serve condiment station next to the fryer, and I discovered entirely by accident that a handful of thin, salt-crusted shoestring fries tucked inside my cheeseburger turned it into something significantly better than what I had started with. The fries added crunch, they added salt, they absorbed some of the meat juices and became briefly soft at the edges, and they provided this starchy, comforting heartiness that made the whole thing feel like a complete meal in a single unit. I ordered every burger this way for the rest of my time living in that town, and when I moved away and could no longer get those exact fries, I spent years trying to recreate the experience. Shaping the fries into little pies — pressing them into a small mold with a bit of cheese to bind them — was the solution that finally felt both faithful to the original spirit and elevated enough to be worth the extra effort.

The patty for this burger will be cooked to medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius, pulled from the heat with three minutes of rest before assembly. Monterey Jack cheese is perhaps the most forgiving cheese in the world when it comes to melting — it flows and coats and turns glossy even before the patty reaches high internal temperatures — which is exactly why the medium-rare specification matters here: if you cook the patty too long trying to get the cheese to melt, the cheese will have been perfect for three minutes while you overcooked the beef. The correct sequence is to add the cheese in the final two minutes of cooking, let it melt over a medium-rare patty, and trust the thermometer. The mini fry pies go on last, while still hot and crispy. Medium rare is the only temperature that keeps everything in its proper order.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
4 cups vegetable or canola oil (for frying)
1/2 cup finely shredded Monterey Jack or cheddar cheese (to bind pies)
instructions: 1. Make the special sauce: Whisk together mayonnaise, ketchup, mustard, relish, white wine vinegar, garlic powder, and onion powder until smooth. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes.

2. Make the bun dough: Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water and milk in a stand mixer bowl. Let bloom 5 minutes. Add egg, butter, salt, and flour. Mix with dough hook on medium speed 8 minutes until smooth. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 hour.

3. Divide into 4 balls, shape into bun rounds on a parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash, sprinkle with sesame seeds, and bake 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool completely.

4. Make the mini fry pies: Using a mandoline or sharp knife, cut potatoes into matchstick fries, approximately 1/4 inch thick and 2 inches long. Soak in cold water 30 minutes. Drain and dry thoroughly with paper towels — this is critical for crispy fries.
5. Heat oil in a heavy pot or deep skillet to 325°F. Fry potatoes in batches for 3 minutes (first fry, just to cook through but not brown). Drain on a wire rack. Let rest 10 minutes.
6. Raise oil temperature to 375°F. Fry potatoes again in batches 2–3 minutes until golden and crispy. Drain on a rack. Immediately season with salt, garlic powder, and smoked paprika.

7. Make the mini fry pies: While fries are still hot, take small handfuls (about 1/3 cup) and press them into a small round mold, ramekin, or ring cutter approximately 3 inches across. Sprinkle a pinch of shredded Monterey Jack over each and press firmly. The heat of the fries will begin to melt the cheese and bind the pies. Alternatively, briefly press the fry portion in a small skillet with a spatula to form a compact fry cake. Make 4 pies. Keep warm in a low oven (200°F) until needed.
8. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into patties 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder.

9. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties undisturbed 3 minutes. Flip and immediately place 2 slices of Monterey Jack on each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. The Jack cheese will be fully melted and flowing. Rest 3 minutes.
10. Toast bun halves cut-side down in the skillet 60 seconds.

11. Assemble: Spread special sauce on both bun halves. Place lettuce on the bottom bun, followed by tomato slices and diced white onion. Add dill pickle slices. Place the medium-rare, Monterey Jack-topped patty on top. Crown with a mini fry pie — the hot, crispy, cheese-bound fry cake should sit directly on top of the melted cheese on the patty, pressing in slightly. Finish with flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve immediately.
